prompt: Which question does a sanity check answer about a new build?

choices.text: Does the build start and do its main pages load?
choices.why: That is smoke: wide and shallow, on every build.

choices.text: Did the change it claims actually work?
choices.why: Right: the fix and its neighbours, and nothing else.

choices.text: Does everything that worked in the last release still work the same way?
choices.why: That is regression, the wide question that comes after.

choices.text: Is the tester following the plan rather than guessing?
choices.why: The word suggests it, but the check is about the build, not the person.

prompt: Why does smoke run before sanity on a new build?
hint: What does a sanity check need from the build?

choices.text: Because smoke is the more thorough of the two checks
choices.why: It is the shallower one; it is first because it is cheap and decides everything after it.

choices.text: Because the standard requires that order
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson cites a rule; the order follows from cost and from what each check needs.

choices.text: A fix cannot be checked on a build that does not come up, so smoke decides first
choices.why: Right: a smoke failure stops everything, so it is asked first.

choices.text: Because sanity checks need the results of the smoke cases as their data
choices.why: Sanity uses the defect reports as its script, not smoke results.

prompt: Checking 1.1, Ana books six tickets, as the defect report says, and then also tries seven. What is the second request for?
hint: What could a hurried fix get wrong while passing the first?

choices.text: A fix that dropped the upper limit would pass the retest
choices.why: Right: the neighbour across the boundary is where a hurried fix goes wrong.

choices.text: It is the retest itself, run a second time to be sure the result repeats
choices.why: The retest is the six-ticket request from the report; seven is a different case.

choices.text: It starts the regression run
choices.why: Regression is the wide run of lesson 10; this is one neighbour of one fix.

choices.text: Seven tickets is the case the defect report describes
choices.why: The report was about six being refused.

prompt: A build claims to fix "a 64-character password is refused at sign-up", against R2's 8 to 64. Which set is a sanity check of it?
hint: The fix, and what sits right beside it.

choices.text: Every case written for R2 and R3
choices.why: That is the regression of sign-up, a wider question for after sanity.

choices.text: Check that /health answers and the sign-up page loads
choices.why: That is smoke; it says nothing about the length rule.

choices.text: 64 characters accepted, 65 refused
choices.why: Right: the retest and its neighbour across the boundary.

choices.text: A 64-character password accepted, run twice on two browsers
choices.why: A second browser is a compatibility question; the boundary on the far side is still unchecked.

prompt: Match each question about a new build to the check that asks it.
hint: Four questions, four names; one name is left over.

pairs.left: Does it start, and do the main pages load?
Do the steps of the defect report pass now?
Did the fix work, and do its neighbours still behave?
Does everything that worked before still work?

prompt: Smoke passes on a new build, then the retest of its one fix fails. What happens to the regression run planned for the afternoon?
hint: What would the afternoon be spent on?

choices.text: It runs as planned, so the failure can be reported together with the others
choices.why: Its results would describe a build that is going to be replaced.

choices.text: It runs, but only on the areas the fix did not touch
choices.why: The build still goes back; a partial run is spent on it all the same.

choices.text: It waits: the build goes back with the failed retest
choices.why: Right: nobody spends hours on a build that did not do what it claimed.

choices.text: It is replaced by a second smoke run, to confirm the build is stable
choices.why: Smoke already passed; it was the change that failed.

prompt: Why does the lesson ask you to keep boxoffice-1.0.py before making the edits?

choices.text: Python needs the old file to start the new one
choices.why: boxoffice.py runs alone; the copy is for the tester.

choices.text: To answer "did this work before?" by running the old build
choices.why: Right: only a build that still exists can answer it.

choices.text: So the edits can be undone one at a time if a check fails
choices.why: A failed check sends the build back to the developer; the tester does not undo fixes.

choices.text: Release notes must quote the old file
choices.why: They describe changes in words; no file is quoted.

prompt: What can Rui's release notes never tell Ana, however carefully he writes them?
hint: Think about who writes them, and what he knows.

choices.text: Which defects were fixed
choices.why: That is exactly what they list.

choices.text: Which known defects are still open in this release
choices.why: Rui lists two of them under known, not fixed.

choices.text: Which function he rewrote
choices.why: His notes name discount.

choices.text: What changed that he did not notice changing
choices.why: Right: nobody writes down a side effect they did not see.

prompt: The notes say discount was rewritten rather than patched. What does that tell a tester about risk?
hint: Lesson 1: who knows most about likelihood, and what makes code more likely to be wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: how the developer changed the code is not the tester's business
choices.why: New code is more likely to be wrong, which is exactly a tester's business.

choices.text: A wrong price, risk A, has become more likely
choices.why: Right: every price passes through new code.

choices.text: The impact of a wrong price has gone down, since the rule is simpler now
choices.why: Impact is the harm a wrong price does, and that has not changed.

choices.text: Risk A can leave the plan, since it was just fixed
choices.why: A fix is a change; it makes the area more likely to hold a new defect, not less.

prompt: After the three edits, the first line the server prints reads `boxoffice ___ on http://127.0.0.1:8000`.
Why does the sanity check of 1.1 start with /health rather than with six tickets?
hint: What would a pass or a fail on the wrong build mean?

choices.text: Six tickets cannot be booked until /health has been asked once
choices.why: Booking does not depend on it.

choices.text: /health tests the discount rule in the background
choices.why: It answers ok and a version, nothing more.

choices.text: The defect report lists /health as its first step and every report does
choices.why: The reports start at the Book page; checking the build is the tester's own step.

choices.text: To be sure the server is the build that holds the fixes
choices.why: Right: on the old build, a result says nothing about the fix.

prompt: A member books five tickets for Hamlet at R$ 80,00 each on 1.1, and the largest single discount, 15%, applies. What total in reais should the order show?
Why does the check of the discount fix also book four tickets as the member?
hint: Which other answer of the same rule sits next to the fixed one?

choices.text: Four is the smallest order that gets any discount
choices.why: One ticket as a member already gets 10%.

choices.text: It is the member branch beside the fix, which must still give 10% off
choices.why: Right: the other branch of the same rule, the neighbour of this fix.

choices.text: The lesson 5 report described four tickets
choices.why: It described five, which got 25%.

choices.text: To use up seats so that the next check starts from a known count
choices.why: Seats are not part of either fix.

prompt: Every row of the sanity check of 1.1 passed. Which statement can Ana make on that evidence alone?
hint: How much of discount did the checks look at?

choices.text: Release 1.1 is ready to ship
choices.why: That needs the regression run and the exit criteria of lesson 1.

choices.text: The discount rule is now right for every customer
choices.why: Two of its answers were tried; the other combinations were not.

choices.text: The two fixes work on 1.1
choices.why: Right: that is what sanity can say, written with the build number.

choices.text: Nothing else in boxoffice changed between 1.0 and 1.1
choices.why: The checks looked at five results; they cannot see what else changed.

prompt: Which of these belong to the sanity check of 1.1? Choose every one that does.
hint: The two fixes, and their neighbours.

choices.text: Six tickets for Hamlet make an order
choices.why: Right: the retest of the first fix.

choices.text: Seven tickets are still refused
choices.why: Right: the neighbour across the boundary.

choices.text: A member booking five gets 15%
choices.why: Right: the retest of the second fix.

choices.text: The confirmation e-mail reaches the outbox
choices.why: Neither fix touched sign-up; that belongs to regression, if anywhere.

choices.text: The shows table fits a phone screen
choices.why: Layout is not near either fix.

prompt: Put the steps of a sanity check on a new build in order.
hint: The cheap question about the build comes before any question about the fix.
items: Read the release notes for what the build claims
Confirm the version and run the smoke list
Try the neighbours of each fix
Record each result with the build number
trap: Retesting before confirming the version risks checking a fix on a build that does not contain it.

prompt: A later build claims to fix "a used order can be refunded" (R6: a paid order can be refunded before the show). Which pair makes the sanity check?
hint: One request is the retest; the other guards the branch next to it.

choices.text: Refunding a used order is refused, and the release notes say so
choices.why: The notes are the claim being checked, not a second check.

choices.text: A used order's refund refused; a paid order's still accepted
choices.why: Right: a fix that stopped every refund would pass the retest alone.

choices.text: Refunding a used order is refused, tried in two browsers
choices.why: Same case twice; the neighbour that could break is left untried.

choices.text: Every transition of R6, from every state
choices.why: That is the regression of order states, a wider run.

prompt: Why does Ana write "verified on 1.1" rather than just "verified" beside a fixed defect?

choices.text: A fix is a fact about one build, and the next build has to show it again
choices.why: Right: the build number says which build the claim is about.

choices.text: The tracker refuses a verification without a version
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the reason is about the claim, not the tool.

choices.text: So Rui knows which file to undo if the fix is wrong
choices.why: A failed fix goes back as a report, not as an undo.

choices.text: Because verified alone means the defect was rejected as not a defect
choices.why: Rejected is a different outcome; lesson 16 names it.
